Course 27

Culture and mind

How culture shapes the way we think, feel and fall ill, and why psychology needs to look beyond the West.

Lesson 1. A psychology that is too "WEIRD"

1 · Lesson

In 2010, Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan pointed out a problem: most psychology studies had been done with people from WEIRD societies (Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic), often US university students, who are a small minority of humanity.

When cultures were compared, some results thought to be universal turned out to vary. Even perceptual phenomena, such as the Müller-Lyer illusion, proved weaker in some populations. And in economic sharing tasks, what counts as a fair offer differs greatly between societies.

This does not invalidate psychology, but it calls for caution when generalising and for studying more populations. Cross-cultural psychology compares cultures to tell what is common to all people from what depends on context.

2 · Example

In the "ultimatum game", one person proposes how to split a sum and the other accepts or rejects (if rejected, nobody gets anything). In Western societies offers are usually close to half; in some small-scale societies, typical offers were very different, lower or even higher.

3 · Activity

Pick a famous psychology study you know and find out who took part: country, age, whether they were students. Do you think the result would be the same elsewhere in the world?
